newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan central bank chief urges damage limitation.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan central bank chief urges damage limitation.

text.p: Central Bank of Kenya Governor Micah Cheserem called on Friday for urgent damage limitation measures after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) halted a key loan programme.

"This is an unfortunate development but we must face it. We must not condemn (the IMF). What is important is damage limitation that will ensure the economy is not severely hurt," Cheserem told Reuters.

Cheserem said the IMF decision on Thursday to let its Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) lapse had seriously hurt Kenya's credibility but he hoped quick Kenyan action would secure a new shadow ESAF arrangement, giving Kenya specific targets to meet before a new agreement on another loan package.
He said the central bank was weighing whether to intervene to support the Kenyan shilling but it was not prudent to attempt to stop a stampede because it might only add to the shilling's weakness.
He said he was concerned at the domino effect of the IMF decision with worries over what the reaction of the World Bank, bilateral donors and whether importers would rush to pay their bills.
He said he expected the treasury to issue a policy statement on contigency measures that would focus on "where Kenya goes from here". He said he feared these would include raising taxes.
Cheserem, who was given a new four-year term as governor last week, is a leading figure in Kenya economic reform process and has been at the heart of economic changes since 1993.

Business leaders said they believed the IMF had sent a very negative message about economic reform by allowing the deal with Kenya to lapse. They added that the reaction from foreign investors would be swift and seen in coming days.
Opposition leader Richard Leakey hailed the IMF decision and said it would hit the Kenyan shilling and investment.

"I'm very pleased the IMF has finally recognised the enormous problem of governance in this country," said Leakey, secretary-general of the unregistered Safina party which campaigned for political reforms and against corruption.
"We have been asking the IMF for a very long time to take this measure and obviously it will hit a lot of projects," he told Reuters. "Corruption was absolutely central to the IMF decision."

Fares Kuindwa, Kenya's head of the civil service and secretary to the cabinet, told reporters on Thursday that one of IMF's problems was issuing new aid conditions once previous ones had been fulfilled and "one never hopes to meet all these".
Speaking before the IMF decision was announced in Washington, Kuindwa said that 90 percent of the IMF conditions for aid sent to President Daniel arap Moi were political.

He said that in 1991, donors urged Kenya to introduce mullti-party politics and then end tribal fighting that rocked Kenya in the runup to landmark pluralist elections in December 1992 but once that was done a new set of conditions emerged.
"When you make a move towards fulfilling one set of conditions, you find another (set). We did not expect (a positive) outcome. History is too fresh," Kuindwa said.
Kuindwa was not available to comment on Friday.
